events.title: Aristotle
events.description: Plato's student Aristotle founded the Lyceum and systematized knowledge in logic, biology, physics, ethics, and politics. He becomes tutor to the young Alexander.

events.title: Philip II of Macedon
events.description: Philip II unites the Greek city-states under Macedonian leadership after his victory at Chaeronea in 338 BC.

events.title: Alexander the Great
events.description: Alexander of Macedon conquers the Persian Empire, Egypt, and parts of India in just 13 years. He spreads Greek culture and language throughout the known world.

events.title: Alexander in Jerusalem
events.description: According to Josephus, Alexander visits Jerusalem and shows respect for the high priest and the temple. The city is allowed to retain its religious autonomy.

events.title: Alexandria is founded
events.description: Alexander founds Alexandria in Egypt, which grows into the largest city and intellectual center of antiquity with its famous library.

events.title: The Diadochi – Alexander's successors
events.description: After Alexander's death, his empire is divided among his generals: Ptolemy receives Egypt, Seleucus receives Syria/Mesopotamia, and Antigonus receives Macedonia.

events.title: Ptolemaic Egypt
events.description: The Ptolemaic dynasty rules Egypt from Alexandria. Large Jewish communities develop in Egypt, and the Greek translation of the Old Testament (Septuaginta) is begun.

events.title: Septuaginta – The Old Testament in Greek
events.description: The Old Testament is translated into Greek in Alexandria, known as the Septuaginta (LXX). According to tradition, it was done by 72 translators. This version is used by the early Christians.

events.title: The Library of Alexandria
events.description: The great library in Alexandria collects hundreds of thousands of scrolls and becomes the foremost research and learning center of antiquity.

events.title: Punic Wars
events.description: Rome and Carthage fight three wars for dominance over the western Mediterranean. Hannibal crosses the Alps with elephants (218 BC). Carthage is destroyed in 146 BC.

events.title: Construction of the Great Wall begins
events.description: Qin Shi Huang unifies China and begins building the Great Wall to protect against nomadic peoples from the north.

events.title: Antiochus IV Epiphanes
events.description: The Seleucid king Antiochus IV forbids Jewish religious practice, desecrates the Temple in Jerusalem with a Zeus altar, and forces Hellenization. This triggers the Maccabean revolt.

events.title: The Maccabean Revolt
events.description: Mattathias and his sons (especially Judas Maccabeus) lead a revolt against Antiochus IV. The Temple is cleansed and rededicated in 164 BC – the origin of Hanukkah.

events.title: The Hasmonean Dynasty
events.description: The Maccabean family establishes an independent Jewish kingdom that lasts for nearly 80 years, with kings who also serve as high priests.

events.title: The Dead Sea Scrolls are written
events.description: The Essenes at Qumran produce and collect biblical and religious texts in caves near the Dead Sea. The scrolls were first discovered in 1947.

events.title: Pompey Conquers Jerusalem
events.description: The Roman general Pompey conquers Jerusalem in 63 B.C.E. and enters the Holy of Holies in the temple. Judea becomes a Roman vassal state.

events.title: Julius Caesar
events.description: Caesar crosses the Rubicon, wins the civil war, and becomes dictator. He reforms the calendar (the Julian calendar) and is friendly toward the Jews. He is assassinated in 44 B.C.E.

events.title: Herod the Great Becomes King
events.description: Herod, an Idumean half-Jew, is appointed king of Judea by the Roman Senate. He is known as a great builder, but also for his brutality.

events.title: Herod's Temple Expansion
events.description: Herod the Great begins a massive expansion of the temple in Jerusalem, making it one of the most impressive structures of antiquity.
